claims.claim: Jobs to be done is the progress a customer is trying to make in a given circumstance — what the customer hopes to accomplish; this is the working definition given by Christensen, Hall, Dillon, and Duncan in Harvard Business Review.
People 'hire' products to do a job: a product that does the job well is hired again, and a product that does it poorly is 'fired' in favor of an alternative.
JTBD makes the job — rather than the product or the customer — the unit of analysis; teams should stop studying the product and study the job people are trying to get done.

Theodore Levitt is credited with the observation that people do not want a quarter-inch drill, they want a quarter-inch hole; the implication is that improving the product is not the same as doing the job better.

A JTBD description captures functional success criteria (objective requirements) and emotional success criteria (subjective feelings, including social considerations); jobs are never simply about function.

JTBD and personas answer different questions — the job versus the person; NN/g treats them as compatible and notes JTBD does not by itself promote empathy or prioritize among users with competing needs.

The design implication of JTBD is that features are judged by whether they help the job, and successful innovation targets jobs that are poorly performed in people's lives, designing products, experiences, and processes around those jobs.
Products come and go while the jobs they were hired for persist, which is why defining a market or a business around the job supports longevity.
JTBD is born out of qualitative research such as field studies and interviews, and it does not prescribe a specific format or deliverable.
JTBD theory was developed in part as a complement to the theory of disruptive innovation; Tony Ulwick (Strategyn) pioneered JTBD theory and the Outcome-Driven Innovation process.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether JTBD replaces personas or complements them.
positions: Some voices in the field argue that JTBD makes personas unnecessary (a position NN/g reports as a misunderstanding).
NN/g holds that well-executed personas add behavioral and attitudinal detail, empathy, and prioritization that JTBD alone does not provide, and that the two are compatible.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows NN/g: JTBD describes the job, personas describe and help prioritize the people, and teams commonly integrate JTBD information into persona artifacts.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The field contains multiple JTBD schools with different emphases.
positions: Christensen et al. emphasize the progress a customer tries to make in a given circumstance, including emotional and social dimensions.
Ulwick/Strategyn emphasize functional jobs and measurable desired outcomes (their page reports 50–150 outcome statements per job).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the shared core both schools agree on — the job as the unit of analysis and the hire/fire lens — and does not teach either school's specific methodology, which belongs to research-method territory.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft calls JTBD 'a foundational concept in Ux/Ui Design' without any working definition or attribution.
The draft claims JTBD is 'a building block for later discussions, assignments, and decisions' in college courses; the reviewed sources support no such framing.
The draft's vocabulary defines JTBD only as 'a foundational Ux/Ui Design concept covered in this lesson,' which is circular and unsupported.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer') corresponds to nothing in the JTBD literature reviewed.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate draft with a sourced working definition attributed to Christensen, Hall, Dillon, and Duncan (HBR 2016).
Added the hire/fire metaphor and the drill-and-hole example, attributed to Theodore Levitt via NN/g and Strategyn.
Added the JTBD-versus-personas boundary per NN/g, pointing to the personas sibling topic.
Added the functional-versus-emotional success-criteria distinction per NN/g and HBR.
Added the honest-limits framing: JTBD is one lens, does not build empathy by itself, and is born out of qualitative research.
